phrases.reasoning: const already signals immutability, so casing signals scope instead: PascalCase means the value crosses files, camelCase means this file made it.

requirePascalCaseExported.text: Constant "{{name}}" is exported and should be PascalCase ("{{suggestion}}"). <<reasoning>> A camelCase export reads local at every call site while being importable from anywhere.

dropUnimportedExport.text: Constant "{{name}}" is exported, and nothing in this program imports it. Drop the `export`: its camelCase is already right for a file-local constant. <<reasoning>> If something outside this program does import it, make it PascalCase ("{{suggestion}}") instead.

requireCamelCaseLocal.text: Constant "{{name}}" is file-local and should be camelCase ("{{suggestion}}"). <<reasoning>> A PascalCase local sends the reader looking for an import that is not there.

requireCamelCaseFunction.text: Constant "{{name}}" holds a function and should be camelCase ("{{suggestion}}"), even though it is exported. A function is named for what it does and it is called, so "{{suggestion}}(...)" reads as an action while "{{name}}(...)" reads as a constructor. PascalCase is reserved for exported data and for components, which JSX needs capitalized.

requireCamelCaseInstance.text: Constant "{{name}}" holds an instance and should be camelCase ("{{suggestion}}"), even though it is exported. Casing carries two signals and they collide here: PascalCase is the older, louder claim that a name is a type, so a PascalCase instance reads as its own class. An instance is a thing that acts, and "{{suggestion}}.method()" says so at the call site. Exported data structures like Map and Set keep PascalCase, because they hold rather than act.
